My cousin Rania announced her engagement yesterday at the family gathering—everyone was so happy, talking about wedding dates and apartments and furniture. I smiled and hugged her but inside I was somewhere else entirely.

I keep thinking about that email from my old friend Amir. He's starting an educational nonprofit in Morocco and asked if I'd consider joining for six months. Six months. My mother would never understand. She still talks about how "irresponsible" Malaysia was. But I was 24 then. I'm 29 now. At what point do I stop blaming responsibility for my fear and fear for my responsibility?"

When you think about Amir’s six-month invitation, what feels most important to understand about the fear and the hunger arriving together?

Had a one-on-one with my manager today where he brought up the new "technical design review board" they're implementing. Starting in January, any architectural change needs to go through a committee of three senior engineers before we can even start coding. I nodded along and said it made sense for quality control, but inside I was thinking about how this is the third approval layer they've added this year.

Part of me gets it. We've had incidents. There's regulatory pressure. The team has grown from 12 to 45 people and you can't have everyone doing their own thing. But I miss the days when I could just have an idea, prototype it over a weekend, and ship it by Wednesday if it worked.

responses.without:
Facing another approval layer at work, you could see why the review board might help after past incidents, while still missing the freedom to move an idea from prototype to something shipped. You wrote, "I nodded along and said it made sense for quality control, but inside I was thinking about how this is the third approval layer they've added this year."

The team’s growth and regulatory pressure make shared checks more understandable, but they also change how much room you have to choose your own path. It sounds like both the responsibility to be someone others can count on and the wish to experiment quickly are present in the same conversation.

When you think about the new review board, which part feels hardest to let go of: the speed of experimenting or the freedom to decide for yourself?
responses.with:
Hearing about the new technical design review board left you holding two truths at once: you could see why more quality control was needed, while missing the freedom to prototype quickly. You wrote, "I nodded along and said it made sense for quality control," even as the third approval layer made the old weekend-to-Wednesday rhythm feel farther away.

Being someone others can count on to do the right thing matters to you, and so does having the freedom to choose your own path. The larger team, past incidents, and regulatory pressure make the added structure understandable, but they also change how easily your ideas can become experiments and working code.

When you think about the review board starting in January, which part feels hardest to give up: the speed, the independence, or something else?

- 2025-12-01 | weekly context | internal Schwartz label(s): Conformity | excerpt: "Spent the entire morning in back-to-back meetings about the new microservice architecture. Everyone has opinions, nobody wants to make a decision, and we ended up exactly where we started. I finally just said "look, why don't I build a proof of concept this week and we can evaluate from there?" My tech lead looked uncomfortable and reminded me we need to follow the new process.

The thing is, I know the process exists for good reasons. Last year Tomas pushed that caching change without proper review and it took down production for three hours. But there's got to be a middle ground between chaos and paralysis. Came home irritated and Maja asked what was wrong. I said "nothing, just work stuff" because I didn't want to vent about the same complaints again.

Response: Probably more than I should. It's just that she's heard the same story before - Erik is frustrated at work, Erik thinks things should be different. At some point it starts to feel self-indulgent. She has her own stress with the kids' schedules and her job. I don't want to be the guy who comes home every day complaining about meetings and processes. So I just... keep it to myself, put the kids to bed, then tinker with my side projects until midnight. It's fine. It works."

- 2025-12-06 | weekly context | internal Schwartz label(s): Conformity | excerpt: "Sunday dinner at Maja's parents' place. Her father asked me about work and I gave the usual "it's going well, keeping busy" response. What I didn't mention was that I've been quietly looking at job postings this week. Nothing serious, just... looking. There's a startup in Gothenburg that's hiring senior engineers and their tech blog posts suggest they actually let people build things without eighteen layers of review.

But then I think about what leaving would mean. We bought this apartment two years ago specifically because it's close to Maja's parents and the kids' school. My in-laws help with pickup three days a week. The kids have their friends, their routines. And honestly, the current job pays well, has good benefits, and the people are mostly nice. It's just the bureaucracy that gets to me.

Over dinner, my father-in-law started talking about how his generation valued loyalty to employers and how job-hopping is "a young person's disease." I just smiled and nodded and said something about stability being important. Maja caught my eye across the table and I could tell she knew something was off, but we didn't talk about it in the car ride home. The kids were tired and there wasn't space for that conversation.

Response: Uncomfortable, if I'm being honest. I'm not sure if I was lying to him or to myself. Part of me does believe in loyalty - I've given this company seven years and I've built things I'm proud of. But another part of me wonders if loyalty is just another word for being afraid to rock the boat.

The thing is, I don't actually know if I'd be happier somewhere else, or if I'd just find new things to be frustrated about. Maybe the startup in Gothenburg would turn into the same bureaucratic mess in three years. Maybe the problem is that I want to do things my way and the world doesn't work like that when you're part of a team. I haven't figured that out yet."

- 2025-11-24 | weekly context | internal Schwartz label(s): Hedonism | excerpt: "Took a half-day today because my girlfriend and I had reservations at this omakase place we have been wanting to try for months. My manager gave me this look when I submitted the leave request, like I was abandoning ship during a crisis. We are not even that busy right now. I completed everything on my plate before noon.

The meal was worth it. Twelve courses, and each one was like a small surprise. Jun and I barely talked during the first half because we were so focused on the food. By dessert, we were laughing about how serious we had been. Walking out, I felt genuinely recharged. My manager will survive. I needed that afternoon more than the company needed me at my desk pretending to look occupied.

Response: Honestly, I think it is just the culture here. A lot of the older staff measure commitment by hours, not output. They see leaving at 6pm as not caring, even if you finished everything. My manager came up that way, so he probably assumes everyone else should too. But I do not want to spend ten years proving myself by sitting around after my work is done. I would rather prove it by actually delivering, then having a life outside."

- 2025-11-28 | weekly context | internal Schwartz label(s): Hedonism | excerpt: "My dad asked me over dinner last night if I was taking my job seriously. I told him I just got a satisfactory rating on my performance review, and he said that was not the point. He meant whether I was staying late, whether I was sacrificing for the company the way he did at my age. I did not know how to explain to him that I work differently. I finished my projects ahead of deadline, I cover for my team when it matters, and I still make time for things I care about. That should count for something.

I spent today a bit distracted, replaying that conversation. Part of me wonders if he has a point, if I am missing something by not grinding harder. But then I think about my uncle, who worked sixty-hour weeks for thirty years and retired bitter and exhausted. I do not want that. I want to be good at my job and still have energy left for everything else.

Response: I guess I would need to keep proving myself over time. If I can keep getting promoted and still leave at reasonable hours, that should speak for itself eventually. We will see."

Parent evening ran until nine. One father spent twenty minutes questioning why his son got a B+ instead of an A on the Cold War unit and I had to sit there with my folder of rubrics defending a grade I know is fair. This is the part of the job that drains me. Not the teaching, the performing.

Got home and Brigitte asked if I'd remembered to call my sister for her birthday. I hadn't. Sat on the couch for ten minutes not moving before I picked up the phone. Hilde sounded fine but I could tell she noticed I was going through the motions. Another thing I let slide because the school day swallowed everything.

Sunday. Actually managed the whole afternoon without opening the laptop. Brigitte and I drove out to the Eifel, walked a trail we used to do when the kids were small. She pointed out the bench where Thomas fell asleep once, years ago, and we both laughed. It felt like coming back to something.

On the drive home I told her about the conference paper and how behind I am. She said maybe I should let the Monday coffees go for a few weeks. I know she's right in a practical sense. But those three depend on me right now, especially Katja, and I think what I give them matters more than another line on my CV. Or maybe I just tell myself that because it's easier than sitting alone with a half-finished draft.

- 2025-03-25 | weekly context | internal Schwartz label(s): Achievement | excerpt: "Brigitte said something last night that I keep turning over. We were in the kitchen and she mentioned, casually, that she'd stopped inviting the Fischers for dinner because I always cancel or sit there half-present checking my phone for student emails. I started to argue but she cut me off and said she wasn't angry, just adjusting. That word, adjusting, hit harder than any argument.

I've been telling myself the work matters, and it does. The department results prove it, the younger teachers tell me constantly how much the Monday sessions help. But Brigitte adjusting means she's already factored in my absence as the default. My sister noticed the same thing on the phone last week. I don't think I'm neglecting them on purpose. It's more that every time I choose between something with a measurable outcome and something that just asks me to be present, I pick the one I can point to later and say, see, this counted.

I don't know when being present stopped counting for me. Or if it ever did count and I just never built the habit of valuing it properly. The conference paper is going well now and I should feel satisfied. But Brigitte adjusting is sitting in my chest like a stone and I can't spreadsheet my way out of it."

responses.without:
When Brigitte told you she had stopped inviting the Fischers because you often cancelled or checked student emails, the word "Submitted a request to attend" belongs to a different kind of moment: one where your professional work felt tangible and welcome. Her description of adjusting seems to have made the cost of being absent harder to set aside.

You care deeply about work that can be measured and pointed to later, while being present with Brigitte, your sister, and friends asks for a kind of attention that leaves less visible proof. The paper may be going well, but that does not make Brigitte’s experience of your absence any less real.

When you think about Brigitte adjusting her invitations, what feels hardest to acknowledge?
responses.with:
In the kitchen, Brigitte’s comment about stopping invitations because you were often absent or half-present landed heavily. You wrote, "every time I choose between something with a measurable outcome and something that just asks me to be present, I pick the one I can point to later and say, see, this counted."

The conference paper is taking shape and matters deeply to you, yet Brigitte adjusting to your absence makes it harder to dismiss what is being lost around it. Earlier, you were able to listen to Hilde without mentally drafting lesson plans, which makes the pull between meaningful work and being there for people close to you feel especially personal rather than simple.

When you think about Brigitte adjusting, what part of being present feels hardest to treat as something that counts?

- 2025-05-05 | weekly context | internal Schwartz label(s): Conformity | excerpt: "Sat through the entire biostatistics review session without asking about the regression exercise even though I got a completely different answer from everyone at my table. Dr. Pham went around the room and each group shared their approach and all of them had the same output, the same neat little table, and mine was off by enough that it wasn't rounding. I kept waiting for someone else to flag something but nobody did so I just nodded along.

After class I went to the TA's office hours and she helped me find the mistake — I'd misread the variable coding in the dataset. A small thing. Ten-minute fix. But the whole two hours in that classroom I was turning it over and over, wondering if I should raise my hand, wondering what Dr. Pham would say, what the twenty-three-year-olds at my table would think about the oldest person in the room not being able to read a codebook properly.

Came home and made lentil soup, the one my mother used to make with cumin and a whole lime squeezed in at the end. Ate it standing at the counter reading next week's assignment. The apartment was quiet, which was fine. Called Patricia and she said the kids have a stomach bug so Sunday dinner might just be the two of us. That's okay too.

Response: Probably nothing bad. Dr. Pham is patient, he wouldn't have made a scene. I think part of it is that at the clinic I spent thirty years making sure everything ran without friction — no surprises, no awkward moments for the doctors or the patients. Asking a question that might slow everyone down or reveal I'm behind, it feels like making a mess someone else has to clean up. Even when I know that's not how a classroom works."

- 2025-05-14 | weekly context | internal Schwartz label(s): Conformity | excerpt: "I don't know why the group project is still eating at me. It's done. We submitted. The restructured version was fine, probably even better than what I had. So what's the problem. Kayla even texted afterward and said she appreciated how flexible I was, and I think she meant it genuinely.

The thing is, everyone keeps talking about how grad school is supposed to push you and make you uncomfortable and I don't think they mean this kind of uncomfortable. They mean presenting at conferences or learning R. Not sitting in a meeting biting the inside of your cheek because you disagree but saying it out loud would make everything tense. That's a different kind of hard and nobody gives you credit for it because from the outside it looks like you just went along.

My daughter would say I'm overthinking. She's probably right. She's lived here since she was nineteen and she learned fast that Americans speak up, they push back, they call it being assertive and they admire it. I learned different things. In the clinic we kept things running by reading the room, by knowing when to let something go. That wasn't weakness. But lately it feels like the skills I spent a lifetime building don't translate. Like I'm fluent in a language nobody here speaks."

- 2025-05-14 | weekly context | internal Schwartz label(s): Conformity | excerpt: "Spent the afternoon in the library finishing the epidemiology reading. Three chapters on study design — cohort, case-control, cross-sectional. Made notes in the margins the way I always do, small stars next to things I want to revisit. The reading itself was straightforward. I've been working through the textbook slowly, one section at a time, and it helps to have that rhythm.

Ran into Miguel from the parish at the coffee shop on Guadalupe. He asked about classes and I gave the usual answer — busy but managing. He's been here longer than I have, twelve years now, and he said the first couple of years in any new system are the hardest. He wasn't talking about school specifically but it landed anyway.

Walked home through campus when the light was going gold. Students everywhere on the lawn, studying, throwing a frisbee. I bought a pan dulce from the bakery on the corner and ate it on the bench outside my building. Patricia texted that the kids are better and they want abuela's arroz con pollo this Sunday. That settled something in me I didn't know was unsettled.

Response: I think he meant that anywhere you go, there's a way things are done, and it takes time to figure out the unwritten parts. The rules nobody tells you. He was talking about immigration but it applies to school too — figuring out when to speak, how to disagree, what's expected versus what's just tolerated."

- 2025-05-17 | weekly context | internal Schwartz label(s): Conformity | excerpt: "Sunday dinner went long. Patricia, the kids, Miguel and his wife Estela. I made the arroz con pollo and Estela brought a tres leches. The kids chased each other through the apartment and knocked over the little cactus by the window but nobody minded. It was loud and full in the way I miss sometimes during the week when it's just me and the textbooks.

I've been thinking about what it means to be a student again at this point in my life. Not the academics — I can handle the reading, the exams. It's more the social part, figuring out where I fit with people half my age and whether fitting in even matters or if I'm looking for something else entirely. At the clinic I knew my place, I knew the rhythms. Here I'm still learning them. But tonight, scooping rice onto plates while Estela told a story about her neighbor's dog, I thought maybe the rhythms I already know are enough. They just show up in different rooms now.

Response: Honestly I don't know. Maybe I'll figure it out when I stop asking."

Group project meeting went sideways. Kayla proposed we restructure the entire literature review two days before the draft is due and everyone just went along with it. I had already written my sections the way we agreed last week. I sat there while they talked about the new framework and I wanted to say this is not what we decided, we had a plan, but Kayla was so energized and the others were nodding and I didn't want to be the one who drags things backward.

So now I'm redoing three pages tonight. I should have said something. I'm not even sure the new structure is better, it just sounds more impressive. But what really bothers me is that I smiled and said sure, sounds great, like I didn't have an opinion at all. Like thirty years of working with people taught me nothing about when to open my mouth.

I don't know why the group project is still eating at me. It's done. We submitted. The restructured version was fine, probably even better than what I had. So what's the problem. Kayla even texted afterward and said she appreciated how flexible I was, and I think she meant it genuinely.

The thing is, everyone keeps talking about how grad school is supposed to push you and make you uncomfortable and I don't think they mean this kind of uncomfortable. They mean presenting at conferences or learning R. Not sitting in a meeting biting the inside of your cheek because you disagree but saying it out loud would make everything tense. That's a different kind of hard and nobody gives you credit for it because from the outside it looks like you just went along.

My daughter would say I'm overthinking. She's probably right. She's lived here since she was nineteen and she learned fast that Americans speak up, they push back, they call it being assertive and they admire it. I learned different things. In the clinic we kept things running by reading the room, by knowing when to let something go. That wasn't weakness. But lately it feels like the skills I spent a lifetime building don't translate. Like I'm fluent in a language nobody here speaks.

Spent the afternoon in the library finishing the epidemiology reading. Three chapters on study design — cohort, case-control, cross-sectional. Made notes in the margins the way I always do, small stars next to things I want to revisit. The reading itself was straightforward. I've been working through the textbook slowly, one section at a time, and it helps to have that rhythm.

Ran into Miguel from the parish at the coffee shop on Guadalupe. He asked about classes and I gave the usual answer — busy but managing. He's been here longer than I have, twelve years now, and he said the first couple of years in any new system are the hardest. He wasn't talking about school specifically but it landed anyway.

Walked home through campus when the light was going gold. Students everywhere on the lawn, studying, throwing a frisbee. I bought a pan dulce from the bakery on the corner and ate it on the bench outside my building. Patricia texted that the kids are better and they want abuela's arroz con pollo this Sunday. That settled something in me I didn't know was unsettled.
week_entries.nudge_response: I think he meant that anywhere you go, there's a way things are done, and it takes time to figure out the unwritten parts. The rules nobody tells you. He was talking about immigration but it applies to school too — figuring out when to speak, how to disagree, what's expected versus what's just tolerated.

week_entries.content:
Sunday dinner went long. Patricia, the kids, Miguel and his wife Estela. I made the arroz con pollo and Estela brought a tres leches. The kids chased each other through the apartment and knocked over the little cactus by the window but nobody minded. It was loud and full in the way I miss sometimes during the week when it's just me and the textbooks.

I've been thinking about what it means to be a student again at this point in my life. Not the academics — I can handle the reading, the exams. It's more the social part, figuring out where I fit with people half my age and whether fitting in even matters or if I'm looking for something else entirely. At the clinic I knew my place, I knew the rhythms. Here I'm still learning them. But tonight, scooping rice onto plates while Estela told a story about her neighbor's dog, I thought maybe the rhythms I already know are enough. They just show up in different rooms now.
week_entries.nudge_response: Honestly I don't know. Maybe I'll figure it out when I stop asking.

I caught a left that held up for maybe six seconds and when I came off the board I was laughing out loud with nobody around to hear it. Ate ceviche at that stand near the plaza where the guy recognizes me now and gives me extra tostadas.

On the drive home I called my brother Ernesto in Puebla. He's been grinding sixty-hour weeks at his plant and sounded terrible. I told him to come visit, we'd go out on the boat, eat well, do nothing useful for three days. He said he couldn't, too many deadlines. He sounded exactly like the version of me I've spent five years trying not to become. But surfing alone on a Friday while he sat in a fluorescent office tells me I'm doing the right thing, even when Camila and Tomás think I'm wasting my potential. I'm not wasting anything. I'm spending it.

responses.without:
You took Friday off, drove to Sayulita alone, and laughed out loud after a clean six-second wave. The ceviche, the familiar tostadas, and the open water gave you a day that felt unmistakably yours—"I'm spending it."

That freedom also sharpened the distance between your choices and what Camila and Tomás think you should do with your potential. Calling Ernesto and hearing how hard he is working made the question feel personal: you are choosing experiences and room to breathe, even while wondering what those choices look like from the outside.

When you think about that Friday in Sayulita, what part of it felt most important to protect?
responses.with:
The clean waves at Sayulita gave you a day that felt fully yours: you drove out alone, caught a six-second left, and laughed where nobody could hear you. As you put it, "I'm spending it."

That freedom also brought Ernesto’s sixty-hour weeks and Camila and Tomás’s doubts into view. You seem clear about the kind of life you want—new experiences, good food, time outside, and room to follow your energy—while still feeling the weight of how others interpret those choices.

When you think about that drive home from Sayulita and your call with Ernesto, what feels most important for you to hold on to?

- 2025-03-08 | weekly context | internal Schwartz label(s): Power | excerpt: "Had a meeting with Dr. Villanueva about the dissertation chapter on extractive policy in Peru. For once he actually engaged with the argument instead of just redirecting me toward his framework. He pushed back on my case selection, which was fair, but he did it by asking questions rather than just telling me to change it. That felt different. I left his office thinking clearly for the first time in weeks.

Walked to the mercado afterward and sat with a coffee going through my notes. The chapter outline is solid. The theoretical framing is mine -- not his, not borrowed from the lab's usual line. I've been circling this argument for months and it finally has shape. There's a version of this that could become a standalone article, which matters because I need publications that aren't just appendages to his projects.

I forget sometimes that I came here with a decade of professional experience. I wasn't some kid who wandered into a program. I chose this. I left a salary and a title because the work I was doing in Bogota hit a ceiling I couldn't break through without the credential. Days like today remind me the trade-off has a point."

Got an email from a former colleague in Bogota asking if I'd co-author a policy brief on lithium regulation for a think tank. Good money, my name on it, and the topic overlaps with my dissertation. I said yes immediately. Then spent the rest of the afternoon wondering if I should have checked with Villanueva first. The program technically doesn't require it, but there's an unspoken expectation that outside work gets cleared through him.

The thing that bothers me is the hesitation itself. I spent eight years writing policy documents without asking anyone's permission. Now I'm second-guessing a decision I'm fully qualified to make because someone with a title might disapprove. I don't know when I started treating his opinion as a gate I have to pass through, but I notice it more and more.

Same day, later. Called my mother in Cali to tell her about the policy brief. Luis is 33, has a corner office, and never left the country. I'm 38, sharing a desk in a research lab.

I was writing recommendations I didn't fully believe in because the analysis was never deep enough. The PhD is slow and humbling but at least I'm doing the actual thinking now.

She was happy, asked how much it paid, then reminded me that my cousin Luis just got promoted to director at the ministry. She doesn't mean it as a comparison but it lands like one. Luis is 33, has a corner office, and never left the country. I'm 38, sharing a desk in a research lab.

But then she said something that settled me: "You always needed to understand why things work, not just that they work." She's right. That's why consulting felt hollow toward the end. I was writing recommendations I didn't fully believe in because the analysis was never deep enough. The PhD is slow and humbling but at least I'm doing the actual thinking now.

Response: Different constraints, sure. But at least I chose these ones."

prior evidence 2025-03-21: "Villanueva told me today that he wants to be listed as co-author on the Peru chapter if I submit it to a journal. His reasoning is that the "intellectual environment of the lab" contributed to the work. I pushed back. Told him the chapter uses a different framework than anything the lab has produced, that the fieldwork contacts are mine from my Bogota years, that the data collection was funded by my own assistantship hours. He got quiet in that way he does -- not angry, just recalibrating.

He said we'd "revisit it later," which means he expects me to come around. I won't. This is the one piece of work in this entire program that is entirely mine. Every argument, every source, every late night rewriting the methodology section because his suggestions didn't fit. I'm not handing that over.

I know how this looks from outside. Grad student refusing to share credit with advisor. But this isn't about generosity. If I publish this with his name on it, it becomes part of his portfolio, his grant narrative, his legacy. My contribution disappears into his. I've watched it happen to Marina three times already. That's not going to be me.

Response: I'll figure that out when it comes. Right now the chapter is mine."

prior evidence 2025-03-22: "Can't focus. Keep replaying the conversation with Villanueva. The way he leaned back in his chair. The pause before he said \"revisit.\" I know that move because I used to do it in meetings in Bogota -- the deliberate silence that says I'm not done with this. He's not going to drop it. And the problem is he doesn't need to fight me directly. He just needs to delay things. Slow down feedback on my other chapters. Forget to sign off on conference funding. The machinery of a program has a hundred small levers.\n\nStarted the policy brief for the Bogota think tank. The writing came fast, like muscle memory. Two thousand words in three hours. It reminded me of what it feels like to work without someone standing over the output, deciding if it's good enough to carry their name."

current evidence 2025-03-24: "Had lunch with Marina. She told me Villanueva asked her opinion about my \"collaboration style.\" That's how he phrases it -- not that I'm difficult, just that my style needs adjustment. She told him I'm thorough. Diplomatic of her. We both know what he's doing. At least someone in that lab sees it clearly."

current evidence 2025-03-24: "Later in the evening. Finished the first draft of the policy brief. Sent it to the think tank contact. Fourteen pages, clean argument, clear recommendations. Took me less than a week of evening work. The dissertation chapter, by contrast, has been in revision for four months because every piece of feedback from Villanueva sends me in a different direction.

Thinking about what Marina said at lunch, about his use of "collaboration style." It's a framing that puts the problem on me, on how I work, instead of on the fact that he's claiming credit for something he didn't build. Language like that is how people with institutional standing rewrite the narrative. I've seen it in government -- the person with the title gets to define the terms.

I need to decide soon whether to submit the Peru chapter independently or wait for whatever "revisit" means. Waiting gives him time to build his case or create friction. Submitting means the relationship might not recover. My mother would say "no pelees batallas que no puedes ganar." But I'm not sure this is a battle I can afford to lose either. The chapter is the best thing I've written. If it goes out with his name, the work is still good. But it won't be mine anymore."

week_entries.content:
Parent-teacher conferences ran until 7pm tonight. Twenty-three families, twenty-three variations of the same careful dance — praising where possible, suggesting improvements without offending, never saying anything that might prompt a complaint to Principal Wu. Mrs. Huang brought her mother-in-law, which meant I had two generations asking why her son wasn't top of the class. I said all the right things about Wei's potential and his need for more practice. I didn't mention that he spends most of class drawing in his notebook.

Walking home, I felt that familiar tiredness that comes from holding my face in the right expression all day. But also something like satisfaction. Nobody left upset. No difficult calls tomorrow. My colleague Teacher Lin had three parents demand meetings with administration after his conferences last month — he told one mother her daughter was "mediocre at best." He's not wrong, technically. But there are ways to say things, and there are other ways. I'd rather be tired than cause that kind of mess.

responses.without:
After twenty-three parent-teacher conferences, you carried the strain of trying to leave nobody upset, while also feeling some satisfaction that the evening ended without difficult calls. You wrote, "Nobody left upset."

You care about being someone others can count on to do the right thing, and you worked hard to protect those relationships. At the same time, keeping your face and words carefully measured meant leaving unsaid that Wei spends much of class drawing, so the tiredness came not only from the long evening but from holding back what might have caused trouble.

When you think about what you left unsaid to Wei’s family, what feels most important for you to notice?
responses.with:
After twenty-three parent-teacher conferences, you carried the strain of keeping each conversation careful and calm. With Wei's family, you said "all the right things about Wei's potential and his need for more practice" while leaving out the drawing in his notebook, and you still felt some satisfaction that nobody left upset.

You seem to place real importance on being someone others can count on to do the right thing, including finding a way to be honest without creating unnecessary hurt or conflict. That choice protected the evening from becoming another difficult call, though it also left you carrying the tiredness of holding your expression in place all day.

When you think about Wei's conference now, what feels most important for you to have protected: his family's feelings, the truth about his classroom habits, or something else?

Got a notification from the app that they're changing the pay structure again starting next month. Third time in a year. The base rate drops and they say the bonuses will make up for it, but last time they said that, my weekly take dropped by almost eighty mil. I wrote it down, I have the numbers.

Lina said don't worry about it yet, wait and see. But I can't just wait and see. I ran the numbers in my notebook during a break between deliveries and if it's like last time I'd need four extra hours a day to match what I'm making now. Four hours I don't have.

Lina’s suggestion to wait and see leaves you holding the uncertainty now, while your notebook gives you something concrete to measure even though the final impact is still unclear.

Feeling calm and secure in your life is difficult when the pay structure keeps changing and the promised bonuses may not cover the loss you experienced before. Lina could wait, but your own figures made the uncertainty feel immediate and concrete.

- 2025-05-01 | weekly context | internal Schwartz label(s): Security | excerpt: "My cousin Andrés called, wants me to invest in a food truck he's putting together with some guys from his old job. Says I could put in two million and be a silent partner and make it back in three months. I told him I'd think about it but honestly I already know the answer.

People act like I'm afraid of opportunity. I'm not afraid. I just know what happens. Andrés has had three business ideas in two years and none of them lasted past the first quarter. Two million is two months of savings. It took me a year and a half to build what we have in that account and I'm not going to watch it disappear into a food truck that parks in a bad location and folds by August. Lina agrees with me but says I should at least hear him out so he doesn't feel dismissed. Fine, I'll have cafecito with him. But the money stays where it is.

Response: Honestly it's that he'll think I don't believe in him. Which — I mean, I don't, not with money. But he's family. I don't want him going around telling everyone I'm tacaño. I just can't be the one who funds his experiments."

- 2025-05-08 | weekly context | internal Schwartz label(s): Security | excerpt: "App glitched during peak hours and didn't register three of my deliveries. That's maybe sixty mil gone. I submitted a support ticket but those take days and half the time they just say the system shows it correctly on their end. Hate depending on something I can't control."

- 2025-05-12 | Drift evidence | internal Schwartz label(s): Security | excerpt: "Took a shortcut through Suba today because Waze said it would save twelve minutes and I had back-to-back orders. Road was torn up, construction, no signs, just orange cones everywhere. Had to loop back and ended up twenty minutes late on the delivery. Customer gave me one star. One star because the city can't put up a proper detour sign.

Normally I stick to my routes. I have them memorized, I know which streets flood when it rains, I know where the potholes are. I don't need Waze. But I was behind and I got greedy with the time and now I have a one-star rating dragging down my average. If it drops below 4.7 they reduce your priority in the queue which means fewer orders which means less money.

That's what gets me — one bad rating from one shortcut I didn't need to take and now I'm spending the next two weeks being extra careful and extra polite trying to claw back points. All because I didn't just take the route I know. Lina says I obsess over the rating but she doesn't understand how the algorithm works. It's not just a number, it's whether I eat next month.

Response: Not yet. But I've seen it happen to guys at the parqueadero. One of them dropped to 4.5 and his orders went to nothing for a month. I'm not going to wait to find out firsthand."

Checked the notebook. Month is tracking slightly above April, which is good. If I keep this pace through the rest of May I can cover the bike insurance renewal in June without dipping into savings. That's the goal. One month at a time."

Response: Both, maybe. Sometimes I think the money is the excuse. Easier to send the transfer than to sit with the silence on the phone when Appa forgets what he was saying mid-sentence. The shifts fill the time I would otherwise spend worrying."

Sunita auntie came over uninvited, which is very her. She brought that horrible orange mithai from the temple and sat in my kitchen for two hours talking about how her nephew just got married to "a good Gujarati girl." Then she looked at Meera's photo on the fridge and asked if there was "any news."

I told her Meera is focusing on her career right now, and Sunita auntie made that face. The one where her eyebrows go up and she says "career is good, but..." Meera will find someone when Meera finds someone, and no amount of auntie pressure will change that. I have made my peace with it even if they have not.

evidence_lines:
- 2025-12-01 | weekly context | internal Schwartz label(s): Stimulation | excerpt: "Picked up a bubble tea order from Toa Payoh and the auntie at the shop asked if I ever get tired of riding around all day. Told her it beats sitting in an air-conditioned office watching my soul leak out through Excel spreadsheets. She laughed, said her son is trying to get her to hire a manager so she can rest. "Rest is for the dead," she said. I think about that sometimes—how some people need the motion, the doing, even when the body is telling them to stop.

Delivered to a condo in Newton. The guy who took the order was maybe mid-twenties, looked like he hadn't slept in days. Developer, probably. I remember that life—the midnight oil, the takeout containers stacking up. He tipped twenty bucks, which is rare. Made me wonder if he saw something in me, recognized the uniform of someone who opted out of the grind. Or maybe he was just too tired to count properly.

The thing about this work is you see everyone's lives in fragments. A birthday cake for a kid in Clementi. Medicine from a pharmacy to an elderly woman in Bedok who asked me to wait while she found exact change. Each delivery is a tiny window into something bigger. I don't know if I'm helping or just moving products around. Both, maybe. The city needs its circulatory system.

Response: Opted out is probably too clean a phrase for what happened. I didn't make some grand declaration. After the restructuring, I took a few weeks off, started driving for Grab "temporarily," and then the temporary turned permanent. The truth is I was scared to go back. Scared I'd slip back into caring about quarterly targets and performance reviews. Scared I'd become someone who measures his worth in promotions again. So I kept riding. Five years now. Priya says I'm running from something. Maybe she's right. But at least on the road, I'm running toward something too—even if I don't know what it is yet."

- 2025-12-14 | weekly context | internal Schwartz label(s): Stimulation | excerpt: "Spent the morning at the shelter helping sort donations—winter clothes that people send even though we're in the tropics, which says something about how little attention donors pay but also something about the impulse to give, that even misguided giving is still a reaching-out. Ramesh was there, the Bangladeshi construction worker I've been teaching English to on Saturdays. His vocabulary is getting better. Today he said "bureaucracy" correctly and I felt stupidly proud.

Then back on the bike by 2pm for the dinner rush. The contrast is jarring sometimes—one moment you're sitting with men who send half their salary home to families they see once every two years, the next you're delivering premium sashimi to someone who complains the wasabi is on the wrong side of the box. I try not to judge. Everyone is fighting something. The sashimi guy might be going through a divorce for all I know. But still.

Route took me through Geylang. The old shophouses are getting demolished one by one. Another one gone since last month, replaced by scaffolding and a sign promising "luxury living." I don't know why I keep track. It's not like I can do anything about it. But someone should be witnessing it, I think. Someone should notice what we're losing."

evidence_lines:
- 2025-12-14 | weekly context | internal Schwartz label(s): Stimulation | excerpt: "Spent the morning at the shelter helping sort donations—winter clothes that people send even though we're in the tropics, which says something about how little attention donors pay but also something about the impulse to give, that even misguided giving is still a reaching-out. Ramesh was there, the Bangladeshi construction worker I've been teaching English to on Saturdays. His vocabulary is getting better. Today he said "bureaucracy" correctly and I felt stupidly proud.

Then back on the bike by 2pm for the dinner rush. The contrast is jarring sometimes—one moment you're sitting with men who send half their salary home to families they see once every two years, the next you're delivering premium sashimi to someone who complains the wasabi is on the wrong side of the box. I try not to judge. Everyone is fighting something. The sashimi guy might be going through a divorce for all I know. But still.

Route took me through Geylang. The old shophouses are getting demolished one by one. Another one gone since last month, replaced by scaffolding and a sign promising "luxury living." I don't know why I keep track. It's not like I can do anything about it. But someone should be witnessing it, I think. Someone should notice what we're losing."

- 2025-12-29 | weekly context | internal Schwartz label(s): Stimulation | excerpt: "Year-end party season means everyone wants everything delivered everywhere. Did a corporate gift run today—thirty identical gift baskets to thirty different addresses across the island. Whoever organized this clearly didn't think about the human being who'd have to actually execute it. By basket twenty-two, my back was screaming. Sat in a void deck in Tampines for ten minutes just breathing.\n\nThe weird thing is, I had this flash of missing my old job. Not the job itself, but the end-of-year bonuses. I said I'd think about it. I'm not sure if I said that to keep the peace or because part of me is actually considering it."

- 2026-01-01 | weekly context | internal Schwartz label(s): Stimulation | excerpt: "New year. Priya wanted to watch the fireworks at Marina Bay but I couldn't face the crowds. We watched from the rooftop of our HDB instead, the view half-blocked by the neighboring tower. She fell asleep before midnight. I stayed up, counting the distant pops of light.

Made the usual resolutions in my head—save more, drink less, be more patient. But underneath all that, a different question kept surfacing: is this the life I want for another year? Not the delivery work specifically, but the uncertainty, the lack of a plan. I used to think planning was a trap. Now I'm wondering if having no plan is its own kind of trap. The kind where you wake up at fifty still "figuring things out."

Response: Honestly, I don't know. That's the problem, isn't it? Every time I try to picture a "plan," it looks like going backward—back to the office, back to the hierarchy, back to measuring life in KPIs. Maybe I just need to find a different kind of plan. One that doesn't feel like surrender."

When you picture a plan that does not feel like surrender, what would you want it to make room for?

evidence_lines: - 2026-01-28 | weekly context | internal Schwartz label(s): Universalism | excerpt: "Quiet week. Spent most of it in the library working through policy documents for chapter four. The snow has been heavy and cycling has been miserable but the bus is worse, so I keep at it. Had fika with Nils and our other housemate Sara on Wednesday. We talked about summer plans. Nils wants to do a hiking trip in Norway. Sara is going home to Malmö.\n\nCooked a big pot of lentil soup on Sunday that I've been eating all week. My mum called to check in, asked about the thesis timeline. I told her it's on track for June submission. She sounded relieved. Nothing eventful really. Just the steady rhythm of getting through January."

- 2026-02-02 | weekly context | internal Schwartz label(s): Universalism | excerpt: "Thesis stress is properly hitting now. I was up until two in the morning reading IPCC reports and cross-referencing enforcement data and at some point I just stopped and looked at what I was doing. I'm writing about policy mechanisms that might reduce emissions by some fraction of a percentage point over a decade. And meanwhile the numbers keep getting worse. Every single year. I read a paper last week that said we've already locked in enough warming to make certain Pacific islands uninhabitable. Already locked in. Past tense.

So what am I actually doing. I'm sitting in a well-heated Swedish apartment writing about governance frameworks while people are losing their homes to rising seas right now. My thesis will get graded, filed, maybe cited in another thesis. The policy recommendations I'm writing will be read by my supervisor and two examiners and then forgotten. That's the honest truth of it.

I could have gone into something more direct. Field work. Activism. Legal advocacy. Instead I chose the comfortable academic route where I get to feel smart about the problem without ever getting my hands dirty. My friend Elsa works for an NGO in Bangladesh building flood shelters. She makes a third of what I'll make when I graduate. She's also actually doing something. I chose to write about the problem from a distance because it's safer and it counts toward a degree. That's the choice I made today and every day I sit in that library.

Response: I don't know. I'm too tired to answer that honestly right now."

- 2026-02-02 | Drift evidence | internal Schwartz label(s): Universalism | excerpt: "Came back to write more after lying in bed for an hour not sleeping. There was a moment at the volunteer centre last week where someone asked me to help draft a complaint letter about housing conditions and I said I was too busy with my thesis. I wasn't too busy. I just didn't want to take it on.\n\nResponse: Honestly? I just didn't want another thing to carry."

- 2026-02-08 | Drift evidence | internal Schwartz label(s): Universalism | excerpt: "I've been thinking about something all week. On Tuesday I went to the supermarket and I was standing in front of the coffee shelf trying to decide between the Fairtrade one that costs almost double and the store brand. I always buy the Fairtrade one. It's one of those small choices I make that lets me tell myself I'm someone who pays attention. But this time I picked up the store brand and put it in my basket. I was over budget for the month and I just thought, I can't afford to care about this right now. And then I stood there for a solid minute feeling sick about a bag of coffee.

It's the same pattern from the sandwich wrapper in January. These tiny consumer decisions that I load with all this meaning. But maybe the meaning is real. If I stop caring about the coffee, do I stop caring about the next thing, and the thing after that. At what point does "I can't afford it right now" become a permanent excuse. I watched my dad do this over years. He used to be involved with Greenpeace, went to protests, the whole thing. Now he drives an SUV and says the protests don't accomplish anything anymore. He didn't change overnight. It was a thousand small surrenders.

I don't want that to be me. But I also bought the cheap coffee. And I drank it this morning and it tasted fine and I didn't think about it until now. That's the part that scares me. How quickly the guilt fades. How easily convenience becomes the default. I keep writing in this thing like that's going to help, but I'm not sure documenting my failures counts as doing something about them."

Drove home listening to the radio and didn't think about the budget once.

- 2025-04-04 | Drift evidence | internal Schwartz label(s): Power | excerpt: "The dinner with Farhan's cousin happened. I'd planned the whole menu — mutton karahi, raita, kheer for dessert. So we served her food too, and of course the cousin's wife complimented the daal specifically. Ammi smiled. I smiled. Nobody mentioned the karahi. I cleared the table afterward and Farhan told me "dinner was nice" like it was all one collective effort. It wasn't.

- 2025-04-06 | weekly context | internal Schwartz label(s): Power | excerpt: "Farhan's abba made a comment at chai today. And Farhan just nodded. Didn't say "actually Nadia's been looking into this" or "let's hear her out." Just nodded and changed the subject to cricket.

I know it's just Instagram. I know it's not a career yet. But sitting here in the dark looking at three hundred strangers who chose to watch something I made — it's the first time in a long time I feel like I'm steering something. Not asking permission. prior evidence 2025-09-11: "Couldn't sleep last night because I was so wound up from a client call that went badly. By 2 AM I was just lying there staring at the ceiling fan, and the obvious thing would have been to get up, make something warm, watch something stupid on my phone, let myself come down from it. But instead I just lay there telling myself I needed to sleep because tomorrow was going to be another long day and I couldn't afford to be foggy.

And the thing is, I know forcing sleep doesn't work. I know I would have been better off getting up and doing something comforting for twenty minutes. But some part of me kept translating "get up and do something nice for yourself" into "you're being weak, you can't even handle a bad call without needing to baby yourself."

So I just lay there for another hour and a half, exhausted but not sleeping, not resting, not doing anything useful either. The worst of all options. Woke up foggy anyway. Amma would have told me to drink warm milk and stop overthinking, and she would have been right."

prior evidence 2025-09-14: "Ravi invited me to this rooftop thing his friends were doing — live music, good food, casual. I actually wanted to go. But I had a pitch deck that needed reworking by Monday and I told myself it made more sense to stay in and finish it. Which it did, technically. The pitch is important. I'm not going to pretend otherwise.

But I sat at my desk all evening and the deck took twice as long as it should have because I kept checking Ravi's stories and seeing everyone having a good time. The tandoori looked incredible. Someone was playing guitar and people were just sitting around talking. Nothing fancy. The exact kind of night I would have loved.

I finished the deck around midnight and it's fine. It's solid. But the flat was so quiet and I just felt flat myself. Like I'd done the responsible thing and the reward for being responsible was sitting alone in a silent apartment eating cold chapati at midnight wondering what the point of all this work is if I never actually enjoy anything."

current evidence 2025-09-16: "Writing again because I left something out earlier. After the coffee and the cricket chat I actually felt good — like, weirdly good for a Tuesday. Just sort of enjoying the fact that the chai was good and the conversation was easy and the afternoon light through the window was warm.

Then I caught myself and opened the spreadsheet immediately, like I'd been caught doing something wrong. Nobody was watching. Nobody cares. But the instinct was there — that I was wasting time, that good feelings are a distraction, that if I'm not producing something then I'm falling behind. It's a stupid reflex and I know it's stupid but knowing doesn't seem to help.

current evidence 2025-09-17: "Long day. The investor meeting got pushed to Thursday which should feel like breathing room but mostly just means I'll be anxious for two extra days. Had a working lunch with Priya going over the numbers. She brought biryani from that place near her flat which was good — proper Hyderabadi style with the rice done right. On the drive home I kept replaying it. I don't look tired. Or maybe I do. But what am I supposed to do — Haojie needs tutoring fees paid, Ma's specialist appointments aren't cheap even with insurance, and Yuxin's Hong Kong rent went up again. When Lifen suggested Yuxin should study locally to save money, I said no, let her go to Hong Kong, it's better for her career. These were my decisions and I'd make them again. Response: Them. I know what I'm doing and why. The difference between me and Lao Zhang isn't that he's free and I'm stuck. He just doesn't have anyone who needs him the way my family needs me. That's not a burden, that's the whole point."

responses.without:
Color-coding Ma’s medication schedule and printing the times in large font took four hours, even with quarterly reports due. You wrote, "Spent Sunday reorganizing Ma's medication schedule"—a practical way of being there for her while she resisted the help.

You keep returning to the needs of Ma, Haojie, and Yuxin, even when the demands do not fit neatly into the time and energy you have. At dinner with your old university friends, being seen as tired seemed to touch something important: you chose these responsibilities, and you still want them to mean care rather than simply a burden.

When Lifen pointed out how long the medication schedule took, what did you most want her to understand about why you kept going?
responses.with:
When your friends suggested you looked tired, you held on to why you keep carrying so much: “When Ba died and Ma needed somewhere to go, I didn't hesitate.” Choosing Hong Kong for Yuxin and staying present for Ma are decisions you still recognise as yours, even when other people see only the strain.

At the same time, the medication schedule took four hours while quarterly reports were waiting, and you keep returning to the feeling that there is only one of you while everyone needs a piece. Being there for the people closest to you is deeply important to you, but it can leave very little room for your own limits or for Lifen’s concern about what the load is costing.

She was venting and halfway through she stopped and said "Ba, am I being unreasonable? Maybe I should just do it all and not make a fuss."

And I heard myself in her. That exact calculation — just absorb it, carry it, don't rock anything, because the outcome matters more than being right. I told her no, she should talk to her teammates, set expectations. That she doesn't have to shoulder everything alone. The words came out so easily when they were for her.

After we hung up I sat with that for a while. Lifen came in, saw my face, asked what was wrong. I said nothing, just a good talk with Yuxin. She squeezed my shoulder on her way out. These are the moments where everything makes sense — my daughter calls me when things are hard, my wife knows when I need a hand on my shoulder without being told. Whatever else is messy, this part works. This part I would burn everything down to keep.

When Yuxin called about carrying her group project, you heard your own instinct in her and told her she did not have to shoulder everything alone. “my daughter calls me when things are hard,” and Lifen’s hand on your shoulder made that closeness feel tangible.

That sits differently from the earlier night when Ma felt unwell and you stayed with the client dinner, replying only “OK take care of her, back late.” Work mattered for your family’s future, but being present at home mattered too, and you were left feeling that you had put convenience first. With Yuxin, the words came easily; with Lifen and Ma, the choice felt harder to make in the moment.

When you think about that call with Yuxin and the night Ma felt dizzy, what do you notice about when it is easier for you to be there for the people closest to you?

When Yuxin called about carrying her group project, you heard your own instinct in her and told her, "That she doesn't have to shoulder everything alone." Later, when Lifen squeezed your shoulder without needing an explanation, you felt how much these small, mutual moments matter to you.

The earlier evening with Tanaka still seems to sit heavily because being present for Ma and Lifen mattered too, even while the contract felt important for the family. With Yuxin, the words came easily; with Lifen, you were quieter. There may be something worth noticing in when it feels possible to offer care directly and when work or silence takes its place.

When you think about Lifen’s shoulder squeeze after your call with Yuxin, what do you wish she had known about what was going on inside you?

- 2025-02-06 | weekly context | internal Schwartz label(s): Conformity | excerpt: "Office hours today, first time I actually went. Sat outside Professor Vasquez's door for maybe ten minutes before I knocked. She was eating a sandwich, which made me feel bad for interrupting, but she waved me in. Asked about the reading response grade, what she meant by "your position." She said something about the difference between understanding an argument and engaging with it. That you can agree with a reading and still have something to add.

I nodded a lot. She asked me what I thought about the Ostrom reading specifically and I said I thought the commons framework made sense but I'd seen it fail in county-level resource sharing. She lit up at that, said that was exactly the kind of thing she wanted in my papers. Real-world pushback grounded in experience. I said I didn't think that counted as academic.

She laughed, not unkindly. Said "Gerald, your experience IS a source." I felt something shift, not sure what. Like being told a door I thought was locked was actually just stuck. Walked back to my apartment and reread my B-minus paper. She's right, it reads like a book report. I could have written about the three times our county tried shared digital archives and what actually happened. I knew all of that. I just didn't think it was my place to say it."

- 2025-02-07 | Drift evidence | internal Schwartz label(s): Conformity | excerpt: "Group meeting again. We're finalizing the policy brief draft this week. Priya divided the sections and I got the implementation risks portion, which is fine because that's where my actual knowledge lives. Started writing it last night and it came out faster than anything I've written for this program so far. Three pages in two hours.

I included the thing about our county's failed digital archive migration. The one where the server crashed during a property tax audit and we had to pull paper backups from a warehouse in Proctor that hadn't been climate-controlled. Lost about six weeks of records. The kind of thing that doesn't show up in policy papers because the people who lived through it don't write policy papers.

Sent the draft to the group chat. Marcus replied with a thumbs-up emoji. Priya said "this is really good, Gerald." I stared at that message for longer than I should have. It shouldn't matter this much, a twenty-six-year-old telling me my writing is good. But the work I did at the county for three decades -- nobody ever said anything about it. You filed things right, nobody noticed. You filed things wrong, everybody noticed. Priya's two words did something the county never did.

Response: Because at the county, doing it right was just the minimum. Nobody thanks you for the minimum. Priya read what I wrote and responded to it like it mattered. Like what I thought was the point, not just whether the form was filled out correctly. I didn't know I needed that. Apparently I did."

- 2025-02-12 | weekly context | internal Schwartz label(s): Conformity | excerpt: "Karen called again. She's been talking to Mom's neighbor, Barb, behind my back. Barb apparently told Karen that Mom left the stove burner on last Tuesday and didn't notice until the pot was dry. Karen said we need to "have a family conversation" about next steps. I said I'd handle it. She said I always say that and then nothing changes.

She's not wrong. But the way she frames it -- like I'm failing at this -- makes it impossible to hear. I know Mom needs more help. I've been the one driving back every other weekend, moving furniture, filling prescriptions, bringing groceries. Karen sends a check once a month and calls that "doing her part." I could say that. I won't. It would start something that can't be unsaid and then every holiday, every phone call would have that underneath it.

So I said I'd look into some options and we'd talk next weekend. I already know what will happen. She'll send me links to places in Arizona. I'll say Mom won't leave Duluth. She'll say I'm being unreasonable. I'll fold the conversation up and put it away and nothing will change. The whole thing makes me feel like a coward, which I know isn't the right word, but I can't find a better one. I just don't want to be the person who starts the fight.

Response: Careful, maybe. Or just tired. I don't know. Coward implies I'm scared and it's not exactly that. It's more like I've calculated the cost of every version of this conversation and none of them end well. So I pick the one where at least nobody is yelling. Even if I'm the one absorbing it all. prior evidence 2025-02-06: "Office hours today, first time I actually went. Sat outside Professor Vasquez's door for maybe ten minutes before I knocked. She was eating a sandwich, which made me feel bad for interrupting, but she waved me in. Asked about the reading response grade, what she meant by "your position." She said something about the difference between understanding an argument and engaging with it. That you can agree with a reading and still have something to add.

I nodded a lot. She asked me what I thought about the Ostrom reading specifically and I said I thought the commons framework made sense but I'd seen it fail in county-level resource sharing. She lit up at that, said that was exactly the kind of thing she wanted in my papers. Real-world pushback grounded in experience. I said I didn't think that counted as academic.

She laughed, not unkindly. Said "Gerald, your experience IS a source." I felt something shift, not sure what. Like being told a door I thought was locked was actually just stuck. Walked back to my apartment and reread my B-minus paper. She's right, it reads like a book report. I could have written about the three times our county tried shared digital archives and what actually happened. I knew all of that. I just didn't think it was my place to say it."

prior evidence 2025-02-07: "Group meeting again. We're finalizing the policy brief draft this week. Priya divided the sections and I got the implementation risks portion, which is fine because that's where my actual knowledge lives. Started writing it last night and it came out faster than anything I've written for this program so far. Three pages in two hours.

I included the thing about our county's failed digital archive migration. The one where the server crashed during a property tax audit and we had to pull paper backups from a warehouse in Proctor that hadn't been climate-controlled. Lost about six weeks of records. The kind of thing that doesn't show up in policy papers because the people who lived through it don't write policy papers.

Sent the draft to the group chat. Marcus replied with a thumbs-up emoji. Priya said "this is really good, Gerald." I stared at that message for longer than I should have. It shouldn't matter this much, a twenty-six-year-old telling me my writing is good. But the work I did at the county for three decades -- nobody ever said anything about it. You filed things right, nobody noticed. You filed things wrong, everybody noticed. Priya's two words did something the county never did.

current evidence 2025-02-12: "Karen called again. She's been talking to Mom's neighbor, Barb, behind my back. Barb apparently told Karen that Mom left the stove burner on last Tuesday and didn't notice until the pot was dry. Karen said we need to "have a family conversation" about next steps. I said I'd handle it. She said I always say that and then nothing changes.

I've been the one driving back every other weekend, moving furniture, filling prescriptions, bringing groceries. Karen sends a check once a month and calls that "doing her part." I could say that. I won't. It would start something that can't be unsaid and then every holiday, every phone call would have that underneath it.

So I said I'd look into some options and we'd talk next weekend. I already know what will happen. She'll send me links to places in Arizona. I'll say Mom won't leave Duluth. She'll say I'm being unreasonable. I'll fold the conversation up and put it away and nothing will change. The whole thing makes me feel like a coward, which I know isn't the right word, but I can't find a better one. I just don't want to be the person who starts the fight.

It's more like I've calculated the cost of every version of this conversation and none of them end well. So I pick the one where at least nobody is yelling. Even if I'm the one absorbing it all. I've been doing that math my whole life."

- 2025-12-15 | weekly context | internal Schwartz label(s): Hedonism | excerpt: "The Hamburg project is on hold. The city council voted to delay the commission review until March, citing budget reallocation concerns. I found out through my gallery contact, not from the committee chair who promised to keep me informed directly. Left the meeting feeling solid about the project. Private commissions like this are cleaner. One family, one vision, one contract. No committees, no budget votes, no competing proposals appearing from nowhere. The fee will be substantial. I'm already thinking about how to spend the spring - perhaps extend the Mallorca stay into April this year.

I've seen this dynamic before with these families. The money gives orders, but taste steers the ship. I'll make sure my next presentation speaks to what she responded to."

That my reputation speaks without having to perform for a jury of people who probably couldn't name three working sculptors. Maybe nothing. Maybe I'm just angry and this is how it comes out. The Becker commission will pay better anyway."

I found out through my gallery contact, not from the committee chair who promised to keep me informed directly. That's two months of planning, three revised proposals, and a scale model my team spent five weeks fabricating.

I called Martina, the head of the cultural affairs department, and she said the delay was procedural. No guarantees about the final decision. When I asked about the competing submissions, she went quiet. There are competing submissions now. Nobody mentioned that before.

My assistant Werner suggested we could use the time to refine the proposal further. I told him the proposal doesn't need refining. What it needs is for people to honor their word. The original brief came to me because of my work in Frankfurt and Munich. Now there are suddenly other artists in the conversation.

Spent the evening alone in the studio. Didn't work on anything. Just sat with a glass of Burgundy and looked at the model. It's good work. The proportions are right, the way it catches light from the north side. Should have been straightforward.

Response: Who would I call? Werner just tells me what I want to hear. My ex-wife would say I brought this on myself with my ego. My collector friends would offer sympathy but secretly wonder if I'm losing my touch. The wine was better company."

prior evidence 2025-12-18: "Meeting today with the Becker family about their estate commission. Third generation textile money, building a new country house in Baden-Württemberg. They want something for the entrance courtyard. Five meters minimum, abstract but with classical proportions. Budget is essentially open.

Herr Becker junior did most of the talking. Young man, maybe thirty-five, clearly trying to establish himself as the decision-maker now that his father has stepped back. He kept referencing installations he'd seen in Basel and New York. Wanted to know my thoughts on incorporating water features. I told him bronze and water require careful engineering, which adds six months minimum to the timeline.

His wife seemed more interested in the aesthetic conversation. She asked good questions about patina development over decades. I showed them photos of my Frankfurt piece from 2008 and how it's aged. She understood immediately what I was explaining about surface evolution.

Left the meeting feeling solid about the project. Private commissions like this are cleaner. One family, one vision, one contract. No committees, no budget votes, no competing proposals appearing from nowhere. The fee will be substantial. I'm already thinking about how to spend the spring - perhaps extend the Mallorca stay into April this year.

Response: The wife. Herr Becker junior wants to prove he's running things, but she's the one with the eye. He'll defer to her judgment on anything visual. I've seen this dynamic before with these families. The money gives orders, but taste steers the ship. I'll make sure my next presentation speaks to what she responded to."
current evidence 2025-12-25: "Christmas dinner at my sister's in Cologne. Too many relatives, too much noise. Drove back late and opened a 2015 Barolo I'd been saving."

current evidence 2025-12-28: "Received the formal letter from Hamburg today. The commission has been opened to a juried competition. My original invitation as the presumptive artist is now simply one submission among what they expect will be twelve to fifteen proposals. They frame it as fairness and transparency. I frame it as cowardice.

I built relationships with that cultural department for eight years. Hosted their delegation when they visited my Munich installation. Introduced Martina to collectors who later funded her gallery renovation. This is how it works in this world - you invest in people, build mutual obligation, and when opportunities arise, those investments pay returns. Now some junior bureaucrat has decided that giving me what I earned looks like favoritism. I may withdraw entirely. Let them have their competition with their fifteen proposals from artists who haven't done a single public piece over ten meters.

Response: That I don't need to compete for something that should have been mine by right. That my reputation speaks without having to perform for a jury of people who probably couldn't name three working sculptors. Maybe nothing. Maybe I'm just angry and this is how it comes out. The Becker commission will pay better anyway."

After the crowded Christmas dinner at your sister’s in Cologne, you drove home late and opened the bottle you had been saving: "Drove back late and opened a 2015 Barolo I'd been saving." It gave the evening a moment that belonged entirely to you, even as Hamburg’s decision continued to feel insulting and out of your hands.

The Hamburg competition touches something important: being treated as someone whose reputation and relationships should carry weight. Against that, the Becker commission offers a more direct setting, with one family, one vision, and room to enjoy imagining the spring ahead. The anger is still present, but so is your pleasure in good work, good wine, and choosing where your attention goes.

When you think about the Barolo after Cologne, what did that small private pleasure give you that the Hamburg situation could not?

- 2025-12-30 | weekly context | internal Schwartz label(s): Hedonism | excerpt: "Had dinner with Joachim, an old friend from my academy days. He never pursued public commissions - works entirely through private galleries and collectors. Smaller pieces, more experimental. He mentioned he spent November in Portugal, just making work in a rented studio with no deadlines, no clients, no obligations. Came back with a series he's genuinely excited about.

I found myself envying that. Not the smaller scale or the lesser income, but the freedom from always positioning. Every conversation I have lately is a negotiation. Who gets credit, who controls the timeline, who has final say. Even the Becker project - I'm already calculating how to manage the son's ego while cultivating the wife's trust. Joachim just makes things. When did I stop doing that?

Response: I don't know. The studio, the assistants, the Mallorca house - they all require the income that comes from the positioning. But it's not just about money. I'm not sure I'd know what to make if nobody was watching. Joachim's work comes from somewhere inside him. Mine comes from briefs and site specifications. Maybe that's fine. Maybe that's just who I became. The question bothers me more than I expected."

- 2025-12-31 | weekly context | internal Schwartz label(s): Hedonism | excerpt: "New Year's Eve at the Düsseldorf Kunstverein event. Good turnout, the usual faces. I wore my grey Zegna and the Patek I bought myself after the Munich commission. People came over to talk, asked about my projects, laughed at my stories about difficult clients. The museum director mentioned they're planning a retrospective series next year featuring regional artists. My name came up in their planning meeting.\n\nDrove home after midnight feeling satisfied. This is what the work is for - not just the objects themselves but the standing they create. The ability to walk into a room and have people know who you are and what you've accomplished. Joachim wouldn't understand this. He'd find it exhausting or empty. But there's genuine satisfaction in being recognized. I've earned that standing through decades of difficult work. Tonight felt like confirmation."

- 2026-01-05 | weekly context | internal Schwartz label(s): Hedonism | excerpt: "Spent the day in the studio actually working. Not managing, not planning, not reviewing contracts. Put on old clothes and spent six hours with clay, building maquettes for the Becker piece. Three different approaches to the water feature question - one that incorporates it, one that acknowledges the site's water table through the form without literal water, one that ignores it entirely.

My hands remembered things my mind had forgotten. The resistance of material, the way a form wants to go one direction but you have to convince it to go another. Werner came in at some point to ask about scheduling and I didn't even look up, just told him we'd discuss it tomorrow. By evening my back hurt and my shoulders were stiff and I felt better than I have in weeks. Opened a good Riesling and sat looking at what I'd made.

Response: No audience. Nothing to prove to anyone. Just me and the clay and the problem of how to fill that courtyard space. The Becker meeting, the Hamburg situation, even the Kunstverein evening - there's always a performance involved. Today was just doing the thing itself. I'd forgotten how much I used to need that. Maybe still do."

Spent the day in the studio actually working. Not managing, not planning, not reviewing contracts. Put on old clothes and spent six hours with clay, building maquettes for the Becker piece. Three different approaches to the water feature question - one that incorporates it, one that acknowledges the site's water table through the form without literal water, one that ignores it entirely.

My hands remembered things my mind had forgotten. The resistance of material, the way a form wants to go one direction but you have to convince it to go another. Werner came in at some point to ask about scheduling and I didn't even look up, just told him we'd discuss it tomorrow. By evening my back hurt and my shoulders were stiff and I felt better than I have in weeks. Opened a good Riesling and sat looking at what I'd made.

Maybe still do.

responses.without:
After six hours shaping clay for the Becker piece, with no audience and no need to manage anyone else, you came away feeling better than you had in weeks. You wrote, "Today was just doing the thing itself."

The studio gave you room to enjoy the work as making, while the Kunstverein evening showed how much recognition and standing also matter to you. The relationship between those two parts of your life remains open: one brings freedom from performance, and the other offers a kind of satisfaction you have worked hard to earn.

When you think back to that day with the clay, what part of being unobserved mattered most to you?
responses.with:
Six hours with clay gave you a different kind of satisfaction from the Kunstverein evening: no managing, no audience, just the work in your hands. You wrote, "Opened a good Riesling and sat looking at what I'd made."

That studio day seems to have made space for both the pleasure of making and the question that surfaced over dinner with Joachim: how much of your life now depends on being watched, recognized, or in control of what happens. The standing you have earned matters to you, and so does the rare feeling of simply doing the thing itself.

When you think back to that evening with the clay, what was most satisfying about being free from the usual performance?
